placements.caption: Figure 6.5 · Measuring a stop.  NASA Langley's helicopter airframe drop-test apparatus. Notice the marked background and cameras: a motion record can help locate the interval over which momentum changes. This photograph supplies no stopping time or force measurement. Credit: NASA, LRC-2013-00602 ·  Source  ·  NASA media terms . Unmodified supplied rendition.

Figure 6.7 · A target is not always an intact trolley.  DART's last complete image of Dimorphos before impact. The rocky surface invites a question our sticking model omits: what momentum might material carry away if it is ejected? This is an image before impact, not a measurement of the ejecta. Credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins APL ·  Source and credit  ·  NASA media terms . Unmodified.

Figure 6.9 · Holding and lowering.  Removal of an older crane during replacement at Kennedy Space Center. The straps exert an upward force on the suspended equipment. To determine that force's work, we also need the equipment's displacement; the still photograph cannot establish it. Credit: NASA/Kim Shiflett · KSC-20210315-PH-KLS01_0032 ·  Source  ·  NASA media terms . Unmodified supplied rendition.

Figure 6.13 · Height need not become speed.  Orion test vehicle and deployed parachutes at the Arizona test site, 13 September 2017. Air interaction can remove mechanical energy from a descending vehicle. The image does not establish its instantaneous speed, whether that speed is steady, or a constant drag force. Credit: NASA ·  Source jsc2022e045303  ·  NASA media terms . Unmodified supplied rendition.

Figure 6.1 · Bringing motion to an end.  Apollo 15 at splashdown, 7 August 1971. Water and air interact with the returning capsule. A stopping-time question invites an impulse account; a question about motion energy invites a different balance. The photograph provides a setting, not the measurements required for either calculation. Credit: NASA, S71-43542 ·  Source  ·  NASA media terms . Unmodified supplied rendition.
